extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, supervisory patent examiners, Technology Center directors, and patent practitioners/attorneys involved in prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance from the MPEP (§804) on making and documenting statutory and nonstatutory double patenting rejections (including provisional rejections), the applicable tests (one-way/two-way, obviousness-type), use of form paragraphs, and when to add related 102/103 rejections or accept terminal disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer cannot overcome statutory (same-invention) double patenting under 35 U.S.C.
rubrics_metrics.description: The filing of a terminal disclaimer cannot overcome a double patenting rejection based upon 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimers are ineffective to overcome statutory-type (same invention) double patenting rejections. Distinguish statutory (same invention) double patenting from nonstatutory (obviousness-type) double patenting when considering terminal disclaimers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory (same-invention) double patenting – identical scope required
rubrics_metrics.description: Use form paragraph 8.31 where the ‘scope’ of the inventions claimed in the patent and the application is identical (i.e., same invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 8.31 must be preceded by form paragraph 8.30 and is used only where the conflicting claims are in an issued patent and the scope is identical. Do not use this paragraph if the conflicting claims are in a copending application (use provisional form paragraph 8.32). Do not use for nonstatutory-type double patenting (use 8.33–8.39). In bracket 3 insert the number of the conflicting patent. If the patent is to a different inventive entity and is commonly assigned, use form paragraph 8.27 to require the assignee to name the first inventor. If evidence shows the patent is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(f) or (g), also make rejections using appropriate 102/103 form paragraphs (e.g., 7.15 and/or 7.19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional double patenting (copending application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use form paragraph 8.32 to provisionally reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 as claiming the same invention as claims of a copending application (conflicting claims not yet patented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 8.32 must be preceded by form paragraph 8.30 and is used only where the conflicting claims are in another copending application and the scope is identical. Insert the number of the conflicting application in bracket 3. Do not use this paragraph if the conflicting claims are in an issued patent (see 8.31). Consider using form paragraph 8.28 as well to resolve priority issues under 102(f)/(g) when common assignment at present does not establish common ownership at the time the later invention was made. A corresponding provisional double patenting rejection should also be made in the conflicting application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory double patenting doctrine (policy basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonstatutory double patenting is a judicially created doctrine grounded in public policy to prevent unjustified or improper timewise extension of the ‘right to exclude’ granted by a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use nonstatutory double patenting rejections to prevent unjustified term extension or harassment by multiple assignees. Form paragraph 8.33 is the heading for nonstatutory double patenting and must precede the specific nonstatutory form paragraphs (8.34–8.39). A timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(c)/(d) may overcome an actual or provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection if the conflicting patent/application is commonly owned or is subject to a qualifying joint research agreement. Registered attorneys/agents may sign a terminal disclaimer; an assignee-signed terminal disclaimer must comply with 37 CFR 3.73(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness-type nonstatutory double patenting (when appropriate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate where conflicting claims are not identical but at least one application claim is not patentably distinct from the reference claim(s) because it is anticipated by, or would have been obvious over, the reference claim(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness-type double patenting parallels the analysis for 35 U.S.C. 103 obviousness determinations; the patent used as the reference is not treated as prior art. Use form paragraphs 8.34–8.37 depending on whether the primary reference is a patent or application and whether secondary references are used. If based on a patent, use 8.34 (no secondary) or 8.36 (with secondary). If based on a copending application, use provisional paragraphs 8.35 or 8.37. Ensure form paragraph 8.33 precedes the chosen paragraph and is used only once in an Office action. If evidence also shows 102/103 issues (e.g., 102(f)/(g) or 102(e)), add the appropriate 102/103 rejections as indicated in the MPEP (form paragraphs 7.15/7.19/7.21 etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Graham v. John Deere factual inquiries in obviousness-type double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: When making an obviousness-type double patenting analysis, apply the Graham factual inquiries: (A) determine scope and content of the patent claim relative to the application claim; (B) determine differences between the claims; (C) determine the level of ordinary skill in the art; (D) evaluate any objective indicia of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conclusion of obviousness-type double patenting is made in light of these factual determinations. Because the analysis parallels a 35 U.S.C. 103(a) obviousness determination, the examiner should follow the same inquiry steps and document findings accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection must state differences and reasons (explanation requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any obviousness-type double patenting rejection should make clear: (A) the differences between the inventions defined by the conflicting claims, and (B) the reasons why a person of ordinary skill in the art would conclude that the claim at issue is anticipated by, or would have been an obvious variation of, the invention defined in the patent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bracketed explanatory text provide the specific rationale for why claims are not patentably distinct (e.g., supply factual comparisons, reasoning tying prior claim limitations to the application claim, and any secondary references used). For provisional rejections, provide appropriate rationale in bracket 4 or 5 as directed by the form paragraph templates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of patent disclosure in obviousness-type analysis (limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure of a patent may not be used as prior art, but the specification can be used as a dictionary to learn claim term meanings and portions of the specification that provide support for patent claims may be examined when addressing whether an application claim is an obvious variation of an invention claimed in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat the entire patent disclosure as a 103 reference; only use portions that define or support the patent claims. Cite relevant case law (e.g., Toro, Renishaw, Vogel) when using patent disclosure to construe terms or identify embodiments that support comparison. Be cautious not to improperly use the patent as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-way vs two-way obviousness tests (when each applies)
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-way determination of obviousness is normally sufficient (ask whether the application claim would have been anticipated by or an obvious variation of the patent claim). A two-way test is applied only when the applicant could not have filed the claims in a single application and there is administrative delay by the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a one-way test in most cases, including when the application is later filed or both were filed the same day. Apply the two-way test only when administrative delay and inability to have claimed both inventions in one application are clearly shown; two-way requires applying the Graham analysis twice (with application claims as claims-in-issue and then with the patent claims as claims-in-issue), and both analyses must compel a conclusion of obviousness to support an obviousness-type double patenting rejection. Shift burden to applicant to show why two-way is required if record does not clearly show administrative delay or inability to file together.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to add 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections in addition to double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: If evidence of record indicates the conflicting patent or application is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(f), 102(g), or has an earlier effective filing date, apply additional 102(e)/103(a) or 102(f)/103(a) rejections as appropriate using the relevant form paragraphs (e.g., 7.15, 7.19, 7.21, 7.21.01, 7.21.02).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make additional rejections when the facts support treating the conflicting document as statutory prior art; for example, if the patent has an earlier effective U.S. filing date, consider a 102(e)/103(a) rejection. For applications pending on or after Dec. 10, 2004, do not make or maintain 102(e)/103(a) rejections if the patent is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) as prior art in a 103(a) rejection. For mutual prior art situations, add corresponding rejections in the other application as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness-type double patenting with secondary references
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness-type double patenting rejection may be based on the primary conflicting claim plus secondary reference(s) (i.e., claim [1] is unpatentable over claim [2] of a patent or application in view of [secondary reference]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 8.36 (primary reference is a patent) or 8.37 (primary reference is a copending application) and insert the secondary reference in the designated bracket and provide an explanation of the obviousness-type rejection. Follow same ownership/common-inventor/JRA conditions as other double patenting rejections, and add 102/103 rejections where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schneller-type (other) nonstatutory double patenting – rare circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain unique fact patterns (illustrated by In re Schneller) justify another type of nonstatutory double patenting rejection even where inventions may be nonobvious over each other, e.g., when earlier patent claims effectively cover and would extend protection for later claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schneller-based double patenting rejections are rare and fact-specific. An examiner must consult with the SPE and obtain approval of the Technology Center Director before making such a nonstatutory double patenting rejection. Form paragraphs 8.33 and 8.38 (or 8.39 for provisional) may be used for this type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph usage and sequencing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 8.33 (heading for nonstatutory double patenting) must precede any one of form paragraphs 8.34–8.39 and must be used only once in an Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate specific form paragraph (8.34–8.39) depending on whether the reference is a patent or application, whether secondary references are used, and whether the rejection is provisional. Insert required bracketed information (claim numbers, patent/application numbers, rationale, secondary references). Use related form paragraphs (e.g., 8.27, 8.28) when required by ownership or priority issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership/common-inventor/joint research agreement conditions for double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: A double patenting rejection (statutory or nonstatutory) may be used where the conflicting patent/application is: (a) by the same inventive entity, or (b) by a different inventive entity and is commonly assigned even though there is no common inventor, or (c) not commonly assigned but has at least one common inventor, or (d) made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on common assignment or a joint research agreement to justify use of a terminal disclaimer or to make certain double patenting rejections, ensure proper documentary support is of record. If common assignment now exists but file does not establish common ownership at time the later invention was made, consider using form paragraph 8.28 to resolve priority issues under 102(f)/(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make corresponding provisional rejections in conflicting copending applications
rubrics_metrics.description: When issuing a provisional double patenting rejection based on a copending application, a provisional double patenting rejection should also be made in the conflicting application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate actions between copending files as appropriate and cite the copending application number in the form paragraph. Where appropriate, add additional rejections in the other application (e.g., under 102(f)/103(a) or 102(g)/103(a)) if evidence shows prior-art relationships between the applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: If conflicting patent is to different inventive entity with earlier effective filing date, consider 102(e)/103(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent is to a different inventive entity and the effective U.S. filing date of the patent antedates the effective filing date of the application, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (and/or 103(a)) should additionally be made in the later application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert form paragraph 7.15.02 (or 7.21.02/7.21.01 as appropriate) to make the statutory prior art rejection. For applications pending on or after Dec. 10, 2004, do not make or maintain 102(e)/103(a) rejections if the patent is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) as prior art in a 103(a) rejection.
